meta.ogDescription: Verified: Porter wrote it on page 70 of What Is Strategy? (Harvard Business Review, Nov-Dec 1996) - not a paraphrase, not a fabrication.

answer.label: Written by

answer.sourceLine: Confirmed in the original. The sentence appears verbatim on page 70 of Porter’s article “What Is Strategy?” in the November–December 1996 Harvard Business Review, closing his section on trade-offs — Porter’s own wording, not a later paraphrase or a tidied-up summary of him.

source.excerpt: Strategy is making trade-offs in competing. The essence of strategy is choosing what not to do.
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced section for Porter ↗ lists the line under “What is strategy?, 1996” and pins it to page 70 — an independent citation that matches the original exactly.

The full text of the HBR reprint ↗ was searched directly: the sentence appears word for word on the page printed 70, immediately after “Strategy is making trade-offs in competing,” at the close of section III.

Harvard Business Review’s own record ↗ and the catalogue entry for Reprint 96608 ↗ confirm the author, the November–December 1996 issue and the reprint number carried on the article’s first and last pages.

No Quote Investigator entry exists for this line, which is itself telling — the attribution has never been contested. The wording is stable across sources because it is short, printed, and easy to check.
source.excerptNote: Quoted minimally. The passage runs on to argue that without trade-offs there would be no need for choice and therefore no need for strategy, and that any good idea could simply be copied — summarised here rather than reproduced, because the article remains in copyright.

author.name: Michael Porter
author.heading: Who was writing
author.metaLine: Born 1947 · Harvard Business School economist and strategy theorist
author.bio: Michael E. Porter has spent his career at Harvard Business School arguing that competition can be analysed rather than merely admired — his five forces framework and the books Competitive Strategy and Competitive Advantage gave managers a vocabulary they still use. By the mid-1990s he was watching that vocabulary get crowded out by management fashions, and wrote “What Is Strategy?” to insist that benchmarking and reengineering are not strategy at all. He is now the Bishop William Lawrence University Professor at Harvard, though the 1996 article bylines him under an earlier chair — a detail that trips up a lot of citations.

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: No rival claimant has ever seriously held this line — it is Porter’s, and the wording is exact. What goes wrong is subtler: the sentence gets separated from the article that produced it, pinned to the wrong edition, or swapped for one of its siblings.

items.why: AZQuotes ↗ sources the line to “Leadership, Strategy, and Innovation: Health Care Collection (8 Items),” p. 1721, Harvard Business Review Press, 2015 — a digital bundle that reprints the article. The citation is not false, but it points at a repackaging rather than at the 1996 issue where the sentence first appeared.

The same article carries a display pull-quote reading “The essence of strategy is choosing to perform activities differently than rivals do” — a different sentence, six pages earlier. Both are authentic, and both circulate under the other’s citation. If a source quotes one and cites page 70, it has the wrong one; the page 70 line is the what not to do version, as Wikiquote records ↗.

Citations routinely credit the 1996 article to the “Bishop William Lawrence University Professor,” Porter’s later Harvard chair ↗. The article itself bylines him as “C. Roland Christensen Professor of Business Administration at the Harvard Business School” — the title he actually held when he wrote it.

misattribution.truthLine: The wording is Porter’s own, exactly as printed: “The essence of strategy is choosing what not to do,” on page 70 of the November–December 1996 Harvard Business Review ↗.

context.heading: Why he said it
lead: Porter wrote “What Is Strategy?” at the height of the management-tools boom. Benchmarking, outsourcing, partnering, reengineering, change management — the article opens by listing them, then delivers the bad news: companies had become dramatically better at operations while getting no better at strategy, because, as he puts it, “management tools have taken the place of strategy.”

The famous sentence is the punchline of his third section, on trade-offs. Porter’s point is that a genuine strategic position forces you to give things up — Southwest declines to offer meals, assigned seats or interline baggage checking; Ikea hands pickup and delivery back to the customer. If nothing is being refused, nothing is really being chosen, and what you have is a preference rather than a strategy.
context.detailsSummary: Why quotations of this article drift
detailsBody: The article contains more than one ‘essence of’ sentence, which is exactly why quotations of it wander. A display pull-quote on page 64 reads “The essence of strategy is choosing to perform activities differently than rivals do,” and on page 68 Porter makes a further, separately worded claim about the essence of strategic positioning and choosing activities different from rivals’. All three are authentic Porter; only the page 70 sentence is the one that became famous, and the other two are frequently quoted under its reputation.

sourcesVerified.claim: The exact sentence "The essence of strategy is choosing what not to do." appears verbatim on the page printed 70, at the close of section III "A Sustainable Strategic Position Requires Trade-offs", preceded by "Strategy is making trade-offs in competing." The article runs to page 78, carries Reprint 96608, the copyright line "Copyright 1996 by the President and Fellows of Harvard College", and bylines Porter as "C. Roland Christensen Professor of Business Administration at the Harvard Business School". A separate pull-quote on page 64 reads "The essence of strategy is choosing to perform activities differently than rivals do."

Wikiquote's sourced section for Michael Porter lists "The essence of strategy is choosing what not to do." under the heading "What is strategy?, 1996", citing Harvard Business Review, November 1996, p. 70.
Harvard Business Review's own page for the article confirms the title "What Is Strategy?", the author Michael E. Porter, and the November-December 1996 magazine issue.
The Harvard Business Review Press catalogue entry lists "What Is Strategy?" by Michael E. Porter, product/reprint number 96608, source publication Harvard Business Review, 21 pages.

Michael Eugene Porter was born 23 May 1947 in Ann Arbor, Michigan; he is a Harvard Business School professor known for the five forces framework, and the page lists "Porter, M.E. (1996) 'What is Strategy', Harvard Business Review, Nov/Dec 1996" among his works.
Goodreads shows the quote "The essence of strategy is choosing what not to do." attributed to Michael Porter with the source work named as "What Is Strategy?".

AZQuotes lists the quote and sources it to "Harvard Business Review, John P. Kotter, Michael Porter, Elizabeth Olmsted Teisberg (2015). 'Leadership, Strategy, and Innovation: Health Care Collection (8 Items)', p.1721, Harvard Business Review Press" rather than to the 1996 article.
